citation: Zhang J, Wu X, Ye X (2025). The effect of plyometric complex training on lower-limb explosive power in adolescents: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in Physiology.
population: Healthy adolescents aged 10–19 years (291 male, 20 female), primarily soccer and basketball players, also gymnasts, volleyball, handball, and track athletes.
intervention: Plyometric complex training (PT) protocols including countermovement jumps, squat jumps, depth jumps, hurdle hops, box jumps, drop jumps, and single-leg variations; 6–9 weeks, 2–3 sessions/week, 15–40 min/session, low-to-high intensity.
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 RCTs (311 adolescents) found that plyometric complex training significantly improves countermovement jump height (MD = 2.20 cm) and squat jump height (MD = 2.13 cm), as well as 20-m sprint time (MD = -0.10 s). Improvements in 10-m sprint time were not statistically significant. Subgroup analysis indicated that intervention durations of ≥8 weeks are a key factor for achieving significant effects.
key_findings: PT significantly improved countermovement jump height (MD = 2.20, 95% CI: 1.46–2.95, p < 0.000001) across 10 studies with 287 participants.
PT significantly improved squat jump height (MD = 2.13, 95% CI: 1.32–2.94, p < 0.00001) across 6 studies with 141 participants.
PT significantly improved 20-m sprint performance (MD = -0.10 s, 95% CI: -0.18 to -0.01, p = 0.03) across 5 studies with 165 participants.
PT did not significantly improve 10-m sprint performance (MD = -0.04 s, 95% CI: -0.10 to 0.01, p = 0.14) across 5 studies with 123 participants.
Subgroup analysis showed interventions ≥8 weeks produced significantly greater jump improvements than shorter durations (p = 0.01).
limitations: The sample was predominantly male (291 vs 20 females) and limited to team-sport athletes, reducing generalizability. Risk of bias was unclear for allocation concealment in 9 of 11 studies and blinding in 4 studies, and sprint outcomes showed moderate heterogeneity (I² = 59%).
